About | Public Data Resources for the 26 August 2026 Nepal Hazard Cascade

# About the catalogue

A living scoping review and data catalogue connecting pre-event baselines, event observations and subsequent analyses to support research on the 26 August 2026 Nepal hazard cascade.

## What this catalogue is

This living scoping review identifies publicly available data and information that can support future investigations of the 26 August 2026 hazard cascade. It connects pre-event baselines, event observations and subsequent analyses, helping researchers identify and access relevant material and build on previous discovery work.

This catalogue is the item-level public record created from that review. It brings dispersed resources into a consistent structure and describes their provider, provenance, geographic and temporal coverage, access conditions, licence information, production method where documented, limitations, uncertainties, and review status.

Planned maintenance combines monthly searches across all eight thematic domains and the source families covered by the review with additional checks prompted by community nominations or newly released or revised material. New resources undergo eligibility assessment, and dated releases document additions, corrections and decisions while preserving earlier inventories for citation and reuse. Completed, partial and unavailable searches are dated in the search register, while the resources and assets indexes present the assessed inventory.

## Catalogue coverage

The catalogue covers resources that can support investigation of the event, its causes and consequences, and the wider conditions relevant to hazard, exposure, and risk.

Eight Thematic Information Domains

1. Spaceborne Earth observation: Satellite imagery, scene metadata and derived emergency mapping products.
2. Terrain, geomorphology, and cryosphere: Digital elevation models, glacier inventories, source-area observations and barrier-lake mapping.
3. Hydrology, hydraulics, and meteorology: Hydrometric observations, official flood reports, climate archives and mixture-flow modelling resources.
4. Geophysics, geotechnical baselines, and soil properties: Seismological waveform recordings, earthquake catalog extracts, structural geology vectors, lithological map sheets, and soil hydraulic property rasters.
5. Land cover and environmental baselines: High-resolution global land cover maps, vegetation cover classifications, and hydrographic network vectors.
6. Exposure, infrastructure, and built environment: Building footprints, interpreted or automated damage classifications, transport networks, road blockage reports and hydropower information.
7. Post-event scientific literature and forensic analyses: Scholarly preprints, peer-reviewed research articles, institutional technical reports, rapid hazard assessments, and competing event hypothesis analyses.
8. Humanitarian crisis reporting and civil protection: Multi-agency cluster situation updates across water sanitation, shelter, health, and displacement, emergency mapping delineations, and government disaster bulletins.

Seven Technical Asset Modalities

1. Geospatial rasters and gridded arrays: Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COG), NetCDF-4 multidimensional grids, and surface rasters.
2. Vector geodatabases and feature layers: GeoPackage (.gpkg), Shapefile, GeoJSON, and KML vector feature layers.
3. Hydrometric and meteorological time series tables: Standardized CSV tabular records and gauge series spreadsheets.
4. In situ field surveys, ground photographs, and damage inspection archives: Ground reconnaissance imagery, engineering damage inspections, and field surveys.
5. Cloud-native geospatial services, vector tile feeds, and STAC metadata manifests: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) metadata endpoints, vector tile services, and WMS/WFS feeds.
6. Data-bearing documents and forensic publications: Peer-reviewed research articles, institutional technical reports, and scholarly preprints.
7. Reproducible computational workflows and simulation code: Python algorithms, hydrodynamic simulation workflows, and code repositories.

Providers

National and local authorities; scientific and technical agencies; universities and research institutes; international and humanitarian organizations; satellite archives; research and geospatial repositories; mapping services; and project websites.

Place and time

The northern flank of Langtang Lirung, the China–Nepal border corridor, and the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli system to the Narayani at Devghat, across pre-event baseline, event, and post-event periods.

## Associated manuscript

The catalogue is the public companion to the living scoping review manuscript:

The manuscript describes 74 documented searches through 24 September 2026 and the first assessed release completed on 28 September, containing 141 resources and 5,883 assets across eight thematic domains. This catalogue provides the item-level resource inventory, while the interactive WebGIS presents the spatially enabled subset.

The online indexes present 141 included resources and 5,883 assets from the assessment completed on 28 September 2026, based on searches through 24 September. The complete assessment and exclusion ledger retains decisions, reasons, source evidence and metadata corrections. The assessed release, search and assessment records, documentation and supporting analyses are archived on Zenodo at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23034746.

## How the catalogue is built

1. 1

### Search

Each search is designed for a defined source and purpose. Its interface, strategy, criteria, coverage, date, and results are documented in the public search register.
2. 2

### Assess

Each record is assessed against the predefined eligibility criteria. Until that assessment is complete, it remains under review.
3. 3

### Review

Eligibility decisions, supporting source evidence and metadata corrections are recorded for subsequent author review and reassessment.
4. 4

### Describe

For an eligible resource, information is charted from authoritative sources and organized into consistent fields covering identity, provenance, coverage, access, licensing, methods, validation, uncertainty, and limitations.
5. 5

### Inventory assets

Files, layers, satellite scenes, and service endpoints belonging to a record or resource are listed as assets. Assets remain attached to their parent entry and are not counted as separate resources.
6. 6

### Update

Later searches identify new or changed material. Entries are added, corrected, superseded, or otherwise updated while their status remains explicit.

## Review method and reporting standards

PRISMA stands for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. It is a family of reporting guidelines: it specifies what a review should report clearly and transparently, but it does not replace the method used to conduct the review.

The search and charting process is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Source-specific searches and separate resource and asset decisions document provenance, access conditions, rights, corrections and limitations.

PRISMA-ScR

The PRISMA extension for scoping reviews. It guides reporting of the review question, eligibility, information sources, selection, charting, results, limitations, and conclusions.

## How to read catalogue entries

Record

An item identified through a documented search. A record remains under review until its eligibility and required information have been assessed.

Resource

An eligible dataset, report, service, codebase, or other data-bearing item represented once in the catalogue, even when several records point to it.

Asset

A concrete technical data file, raster grid, vector layer, time series table, in situ survey archive, cloud service endpoint, document, or code repository belonging to one of the seven technical asset modalities. It is attached to its parent resource or candidate record.

Included

The resource has completed catalogue eligibility assessment and is retained in the assessed inventory. Inclusion does not independently validate its scientific content or establish permission to redistribute third-party material.

Under review

The item has been identified, but its eligibility or required information is still being assessed.

## Eligibility

Resources are assessed against criteria defined for the living scoping review.

### Eligible

- Data assets spanning any of the seven technical asset modalities across the eight thematic information domains (including satellite rasters, vector layers, hydrometric telemetry, damage surveys, cloud-native services, forensic publications, and reproducible simulation code).
- Resources that inform documentation, investigation, exposure, risk or response within the review scope, including relevant regional and global baselines.
- Resources available without charge through direct access, free registration, or a transparent no-cost request route.
- Resources in any language.

### Not eligible

- Paid or private holdings and resources with an opaque access process.
- Resources with no demonstrable connection to the review scope.
- Commentary or duplicate news coverage containing no unique data.

## Evidence classification

Each reviewed resource is classified by the kind of evidence it provides.

Observed

Measurements, field observations, instrument records, or source imagery.

Interpreted

Human-interpreted mapping, classification, or analysis derived from observations.

Automated

Outputs produced principally through automated detection or classification.

Modelled

Simulations, estimates, forecasts, or model-based reconstructions.

Baseline

Pre-event or contextual physical and environmental conditions.

Exposure

Population, infrastructure, land use, services, or other elements potentially affected.

Mixed

A resource containing more than one evidence class.

## With respect and solidarity

We extend our deepest sympathy to the people and communities affected by the 26 August 2026 disaster, especially to those who lost family members and loved ones, sustained injuries, were displaced, or suffered the loss of homes, livelihoods, infrastructure, and cultural or natural heritage. We stand in solidarity with the people of Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, and with every community across the affected region.

This research is offered in the hope that it can strengthen scientific understanding, risk awareness, preparedness, and future efforts to prevent or mitigate such hazards and catastrophes.

# Bhote Koshi Flash Flood Impact and Exposure Atlas

A glacier collapse north of Langtang Lirung sent a debris flood down the Chhochen Khola, the Lhende, the Bhote Koshi and the Trishuli on 26 August 2026, from Tibet through Rasuwagadhi to Devighat and beyond. This atlas places every reported impact on that line and against the terrain - a source-cited damage register paired with a Copernicus-DEM height-above-channel exposure envelope.

Data Package

ZIP v13 (37.5 MB) - 22 GeoPackages + 25 FGDC metadata sidecars + 27 CSVs + 12 GeoJSONs + 3 GeoTIFFs. Copernicus EMS EMSR927 observed event extent and damage grading for FOUR AOIs - the three corridor AOIs (942.00 ha, the validation set) and, new in v13, Phosretar downstream of Devighat (422.56 ha, 563 graded buildings, 21 bridges, env_tested=False) - + envelope validation tables + the HOT full-corridor observed flood extent (ODbL 1.0, separate terms) with its CC-BY validation table + two Sentinel-1 radar non-detections at the barrier lake with sigma0 change rasters, search envelopes, probes and dark clusters + Planet scene coverage with no imagery redistributed + modelled barrier-lake pool + HAND GeoTIFF + PDF + README with version history + manifest + verification log

Shapefile Bundle

ZIP (1.7 MB) - 23 ESRI Shapefiles exported from the v13 GeoPackages: corridor channel and envelope bands, exposed settlements, bridges and road, damage register, barrier lake and modelled pools, upstream drainage, Copernicus EMS observed extent and damage grading (4 AOIs), both SAR non-detection sets, Planet scene coverage, and the HOT observed extent (ODbL, separate terms). Field names truncated to 10 characters with a crosswalk CSV; the GeoPackages remain the citable geometry.

PDF Report

Active Hazard The lower lake has drained; MWR now measures a 1.4 Mm³ crater 5.6 km upstream as of 31 Aug

A second flood wave ran the corridor on 30 August, and Beijing told Nepal it was not a lake burst. A surge passed Dhunche at about 03:30 NPT; levels had receded by afternoon (The Rising Nepal / RSS). At about 11:30 NPT the Trishuli took the 130 m Ghyalchowk–Charaudi suspension bridge in Gorkha — the third suspension bridge lost, and itself the replacement route for the Dhawadighat bridge lost on 26 August (RSS). Nepal asked Beijing and was told the increased upstream flow came from an avalanche, not a breach (MoFA via The Rising Nepal); NDRRMA chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety confirms Sunday’s phone alerts followed a Chinese notification of increased flow (AP via NPR). Earlier the same day the Prithvi Highway subsided at Krishnabhir in Dhading, blocking the Muglin–Kathmandu section (The Kathmandu Post). Both failures lie beyond the 62.4 km corridor mapped here and outside all four EMS AOIs, and neither is added to the damage register: no source gives a coordinate, and this page does not geolocate from news text.

The lower lake has fully drained — but the dam is described as less stable, not more. China’s Ministry of Water Resources said on Sunday 30 August that the impounded water has been almost completely discharged and is flowing normally through natural channels, its hydrological emergency monitoring team cited by China Daily (The Kathmandu Post, 30 August). Its Saturday-evening remote-sensing analysis had already found the lake reduced, with risk manageable; G216 repair at Gyirong Port resumed on that basis (CGTN, 30 August). Its measured area fell from 120,000 m² on 27 August to 99,000 m² on 29 August (MWR via CCTV and Reuters); NDRRMA’s independent 0.11 km² for 27 August, from Planet Labs and Landsat via the Stimson Center, agrees to within 9 percent. The dam itself came down carrying ice and snow, leaving it high in water content and soft underfoot, and China Anneng now runs slope radar and drones on it around the clock so downstream teams can be pulled if it moves.

The upper feature is not a lake — MWR calls it an impact crater, and it now has an area, a volume and an altitude. China’s Ministry of Water Resources places it about 5.6 km upstream of the barrier lake at roughly 3,700 m, some 800 m higher than the lake, and at 11:23 on Sunday 30 August measured its water surface at 108,000 m² — down 19,000 m² from 07:00 — holding about 1,400,000 m³, with water flowing out continuously about 180 m below its dam (Xinhua, 30 August 20:28 Beijing time). Three further water-accumulation areas within 2.5 km downstream total under 70,000 m². The same MWR assessment reaches this page twice with two different names and two different days. China Daily, relayed by KathmanduPati on 31 August, calls the feature an erosion pit rather than an impact crater, places it on the Chhuchen Khola above its confluence with the Purepu Tsangpo, and dates the 108,000 m² reading to 11:23 on Saturday 29 August, not Sunday 30 August. Every figure matches — 1.4 Mm³, 5.6 km, 800 m, the 19,000 m² fall from 07:00, the three areas under 70,000 m² — so this is one assessment, not two, and the day it was taken is unresolved. The Sunday reading is retained here because Xinhua carried it on a 30 August dateline; the conflict is logged rather than settled. MWR says the crater and those three areas still pose risk hazards and require continued monitoring, so the hazard window does not close with the lower lake. This supersedes Chen Hongqi of the Ministry of Natural Resources’ Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, who on 29 August put the water at the foot of the collapse at over 120,000 m², depth not established and no visible outlet (Reuters), and it is the first agency reading against which Nitesh Khadka of the Chinese Academy of Sciences can be set: his 30 August account of more than half the upper water having run out (The Kathmandu Post) is neither confirmed nor contradicted by a 15 percent area loss over four hours. A Chinese geohazards expert warns over 100 glacial lakes in the area could pose a threat. MWR describes the lower lake as straddling the China–Nepal border, which makes the Nepal-versus-China placement dispute a false dichotomy rather than a settled question.

A third barrier lake formed on 29 August on the Nepali side, and has already breached. MWR reports it about 2.8 km downstream of the previous one, formed by a landslide on the Nepali side, its dam since breached by upstream flow and the channel back in a flowing state on drone footage and panoramic imagery (Xinhua, 30 August). That sits awkwardly against what Nepal was told — that Sunday’s increased flow came from an avalanche, not a breach — and no source reconciles the two accounts or timestamps the breach. It is not mapped here: no coordinate, area or volume has been published for it, and this atlas does not place a feature from a distance-along-river.

Nothing observed shows any of these features. None is mapped in this package: the marker is a single inferred point for the lower feature (medium confidence) and the two pool polygons are terrain-modelled screening surfaces, not observed water. Both overstate the lower lake on every published date — 19.1 ha and 29.5 ha against 9.9 ha and 12.0 ha — and have not been redrawn, because MWR published an area, not a geometry, and this atlas does not synthesise geometry from a scalar. ## Overview What Happened, and What This Records

At 02:52:10 UTC on 26 August 2026 (08:37 Nepal time) a glacier collapsed on the north side of Langtang Lirung and Tsangbu Ri. Nepali officials had initially attributed the flood to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake; satellite imagery and seismology have since converged on an ice avalanche — an unnamed glacier roughly 610 m wide that fell about 1,200 m, most of it melting from the friction of the impact. This atlas pairs a source-cited register of reported damage with a Copernicus-DEM height-above-channel envelope, so every claim about what was hit can be checked against where it sits relative to the river. Sixteen damage records, 13 exposed settlements, 38 main-stem bridge crossings, 28.5 km of the Pasang Lhamu Highway and five of the six damaged Nepal Electricity Authority facilities are placed on the same 62 km line.

## Why This Dataset The Problem It Solves

In the first days after a Himalayan flood, the damage picture arrives as a list of place names in news copy and agency statements. It is rarely georeferenced, almost never height-referenced, and impossible to reconcile with what the terrain would allow. That makes it hard to answer the questions responders actually have: how far above the river was this settlement, how much of the valley floor could plausibly have been reached, and how many people lived on it.

This product does the reconciliation. Every reported impact is georeferenced from a named open feature — not from the news text — and then intersected against a terrain surface. Where the two disagree, the disagreement is published rather than smoothed over: Dhunche's reported flooding turns out to be tributary flooding 733 m above the main stem, and the Trishuli 3B hub substation sits 20 km from the river, where direct inundation is implausible.

## Methodology How It Was Built

Flood path. The main stem was assembled from OpenStreetMap `waterway=river` ways named Bhote Koshi, Trishuli River, Trishuli Ganga River and Trisuli, linemerged, and the longest continuous component taken: 62.42 km from 28.2781 N, 85.3770 E at the border to 27.8666 N, 85.1127 E at Devighat.

HAND(pixel) = DEM(pixel) − DEM(nearest channel cell) envelope(b) = { HAND ≤ b m } ∩ { distance to channel ≤ 2,500 m }, b ∈ {10, 20, 40, 80}

Copernicus GLO-30 tiles N27_00_E085 and N28_00_E085 were mosaicked to the corridor at roughly 29 m pixels. The channel was rasterized, a Euclidean distance transform with index return gave every pixel the elevation of its nearest channel cell, and subtraction produced the height-above-channel surface. The 80 m band is not arbitrary: reporting records floodwaters reaching settlements about 80 m (270 ft) above river level, and the chief customs officer at Timure described a wave “rising like a wave nearly 100 metres high”.

Population. WorldPop 2020 UN-adjusted unconstrained counts were reprojected onto the DEM grid by density-preserving bilinear resampling. The constrained BSGM raster was tested first and rejected: it sums to 25.3 million against a UN 2020 total of 29.1 million, has only 272,253 valid pixels nationally, and places 35,449 people in a single 92 m cell.

Damage register. Each of the 16 records is georeferenced independently of the damage claim, from OSM, Wikidata, Wikipedia coordinates or Wikipedia GeoSearch, and carries that source, a `location_confidence` flag and an evidence URL. Nothing is inferred: where a coordinate could not be established from a named open feature, that is recorded rather than estimated.

## Key Findings What the Data Shows

- USGS reclassified the trigger from earthquake to landslide. Event us7000tbwb carries `event-type: landslide`, Ms 5.2 and a fixed 0 km depth — the signature of a surface mass movement. The distinction is not academic: an earthquake-triggered avalanche and a spontaneous glacier collapse imply different monitoring regimes.
- The valley floor is thin, and almost everything is on it. Only 39.4 km² of the 62 km corridor lies within 80 m of the river, and 8.8 km² within 10 m. Into that ribbon fall 13 mapped settlements, 28.5 km of the Pasang Lhamu Highway, 38 main-stem bridge crossings and five of the six damaged NEA facilities.
- 17,167 residents in the 80 m envelope — a floor, not a ceiling. WorldPop under-counts these hill districts against the 2021 census by 27 percent in Nuwakot and 37 percent in Rasuwa; the district-ratio adjustment gives roughly 23,700. Exposure is concentrated: 15,850 of the 17,167 are in Nuwakot and 14,191 in Bidur alone.
- The road and the river are the same corridor. The Department of Roads reported the entire 42 km Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi stretch destroyed. Measured along the river that reach is 45.5 km — within 9 percent, which corroborates the figure. The 16 km Syaphrubesi–border section, rebuilt to two lanes with a Chinese grant after the 2025 floods, was swept away again.
- 231 MW of hydropower on one glaciated headwater. Rasuwagadhi (111 MW, river km 5.0), Chilime (22 MW, powerhouse at km 12.4 and 7 m above the channel), Upper Trishuli 3A (60 MW, km 39.0, on the channel), Trishuli (24 MW, km 53.9) and Devighat (14.1 MW, km 58.9) all sit inside the envelope. Cascade siting concentrated the risk the flood realised.
- The steepest reach is where people lived closest to the water. Between Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi the channel loses 348 m in 14.7 km, and Timure and Syabrubesi sit just 40 m and 37 m above it on valley floors a few hundred metres wide. Timure was hit first, about three river kilometres from the border, and much of it was gone within moments.

## Analytical Uses What You Can Do With This

- Search and relief sequencing — the register orders every reported impact by river chainage, so the order in which the wave arrived is explicit and the envelope shows which ground between the named places is low enough to have been reached.
- Reconstruction siting — height above channel is the single most useful number for deciding what to rebuild where. Timure sat 40 m above the channel and was still destroyed; that is the design constraint.
- Hydropower cascade risk review — five NEA schemes on one glaciated headwater, all inside the envelope, is a portfolio-level exposure question rather than five engineering ones.
- Transboundary early warning — source, tributary and first settlement lie in three jurisdictions within 25 km. The corridor geometry quantifies how much warning time a Lhende Khola monitoring station would buy downstream.
- Method transfer — the height-above-channel workflow needs only a public DEM and a river centreline, so it can be run for any Himalayan valley before an event rather than after one.

## Limitations Known Caveats

- The envelope is an exposure surface, not an observed inundation extent — though observed extents now exist for most of the corridor. The HOT extent of 27 August covers 31.71 km² and validates the 80 m band at 93.7 percent within the modelled reach (see Validation, above); it ships under ODbL 1.0 as a separate layer. The barrier lake lies outside it and its pool polygons remain modelled. Copernicus EMS EMSR927 released grading products on 27 August–2 September covering Syapru Besi, Timure, Bidur and — downstream of the corridor, untested — Phosretar, and they ship in the package as `ems_observed_event`. The three corridor AOIs cover 942.00 ha of a 39.4 km² corridor, so everywhere else — and for the barrier lake — the surfaces here remain terrain-modelled. Note also that the envelope's agreement with observed damage is not uniform: it separates damaged from undamaged ground well at Syapru Besi and Timure and poorly at Bidur, where the valley is broad. EMS types its polygons as mass movement, not standing water, and the activation carries no delineation product. Planet Labs has published post-event imagery of the corridor, but under a CC-BY-NC licence, so it is not usable in this openly licensed dataset.
- Casualty and missing figures are still moving. Reported deaths ran 8 → 22 → 95 → 157 → 177 across the first 36 hours, and missing totals have been reported inconsistently: the Prime Minister's Office gives 484 tourists out of contact (391 foreign, 93 Nepali) while NDRRMA gives 579 travellers (466 foreign, 113 Nepali). Both are reproduced here with their source rather than averaged. Every figure is attributed and time-stamped; none is final.
- WorldPop under-counts these districts by 37 percent in Rasuwa and 27 percent in Nuwakot against the 2021 census. The 17,167 figure is a lower bound; the district-ratio adjustment gives about 23,700.
- The DEM is a surface model and predates the event. GLO-30 is a DSM, so canopy and buildings raise valley-floor heights in forested gorges, and it records the pre-flood channel — the bed has since been reworked by debris.
- Two hydropower coordinates are inferred from capacity and position. Rasuwagadhi and Upper Trishuli 3A are not named in OSM, have no Wikipedia coordinate and postdate the 2021 WRI power plant database; both were matched to unlabelled Wikidata items and flagged `location_confidence=medium`.
- OSM completeness here is uneven. Bridges are almost never named, the Rasuwagadhi customs post carries no border-control tag at all, and transliterations differ from those used in reporting. Absence from OSM is not evidence of absence on the ground.
- Scope stops at Devighat, and the event did not. The corridor ends at river km 62.4 because that is the reach where structural damage was reported. Bodies have since been recovered in Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, Tanahun and East Nawalparasi, hundreds of kilometres further down the Trishuli and Narayani, and this is now measured rather than inferred: 15.16 km² of observed flooding — 47.8 percent of it — lies beyond the mapped corridor, reaching 54.8 km past Devighat to 84.5564 E. The envelope therefore covers roughly half the affected extent, not the three-quarters previously stated here, and every exposure figure on this page is a lower bound on extent as well as on population.

An observed extent for the whole corridor now exists, and the 80 m threshold survives it. The Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team has published a flood extent for 27 August covering the full Bhote Koshi and Trishuli, photo-interpreted from drone, Landsat, PlanetScope and Sentinel imagery — 31.71 km², against the 9.42 km² Copernicus EMS mapped across three areas of interest (HDX `hot_flood_npl`, via International Charter activation 1052). Twice the area, a different sensor mix, a different interpreter, the same threshold — which is about as good as independent replication gets on a four-day-old event. The last column runs the other way on purpose: only 39.4 percent of the 80 m band held observed water, because the band is a screening surface for what the terrain permits, not a prediction of what was wetted. The caveat below carries over unchanged — the band separates damaged from undamaged ground well in the upstream gorge and poorly in the broad Bidur valley, and the headline number should never be quoted without it.

This layer is ODbL 1.0, not the page default. A derivative of an ODbL database stays ODbL, and converting it to a shapefile does not change that, so it ships as its own file joined to nothing — the package is a Collective Database and share-alike reaches the `hot_*` files alone. Attribution: HOT / OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0. The validation table above is CC-BY, since aggregate statistics are a Produced Work rather than a database. It does not touch the barrier lake, which lies outside the extent, outside HOT’s area of interest and outside its 1 km corridor: the pool polygons remain modelled.

The earlier test, against Copernicus EMS. Until 27 August this atlas had no observed extent to check itself against. Copernicus EMS Rapid Mapping activation EMSR927 has published grading products for three areas inside the corridor — AOI01 Syapru Besi (river km 13.8, WorldView-3) and AOI02 Timure (river km 2.3, Legion), both photo-interpreted from imagery acquired 27 August 05:05 UTC. Timure is carried here at EMS grading version 2, re-delivered 28 August 17:10 UTC, which revised its mapped polygon up from 125.875 ha to 129.361 ha; Syapru Besi remains at v1. That gives a first independent test of whether the 80 m height-above-channel band actually bounds the damage.

One caveat before the numbers: EMS types the mapped surface as `event_type: 6-Mass Movement`, `obj_desc: Landslide`. It is the scoured and debris-covered ground the flow left behind, not a standing water extent, and the activation carries no delineation product. It is nonetheless an observed footprint, which is what the terrain surface here was standing in for.

| Test | EMS total | Inside 80 m band | Share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observed event area | 942.00 ha | 913.34 ha | 97.0% |
| Buildings graded Destroyed | 3,174 | 3,150 | 99.2% |
| Buildings graded Damaged | 311 | 311 | 100.0% |
| Buildings graded Possibly damaged | 437 | 433 | 99.1% |
| Bridges graded Destroyed | 30 | 30 | 100.0% |
| Bridges graded Possibly damaged | 2 | 2 | 100.0% |
| Road graded Destroyed | 56.76 km | 56.14 km | 98.9% |
| Road graded Possibly damaged | 10.23 km | 9.80 km | 95.9% |
| Graded facility area (all grades) | 34.40 ha | 34.40 ha | 100.0% |
| Road graded No visible damage (control) | 86.20 km | 64.38 km | 74.7% |

The last row is the one that matters. If the 80 m band simply swallowed everything near the river it would contain the undamaged road too; instead it holds 98.9 percent of the destroyed road and 74.7 percent of the road EMS could see no damage on. The band discriminates, but by 24 points, not by the near-total margin the headline alone implies — and the margin is carried almost entirely by the upstream gorge. At Syapru Besi and Timure the undamaged-road share inside the band is a small fraction; at Bidur, where the valley is broad, most ground of any kind sits below 80 m above the river, so there the band behaves closer to a floodplain mask than a damage predictor. 97.0 percent must not be quoted without that. Tightening the band costs coverage quickly — the observed area falls to 90.6 percent inside 40 m, 69.6 percent inside 20 m and 42.3 percent inside 10 m — which is consistent with the reported run-up rather than with a shallow overbank flood.

The 3.0 percent of observed area outside the band is upslope scour and run-up on the valley walls. A horizontal height-above-channel plane cannot represent that, and this is the honest limit of the method: it screens the valley floor well and says nothing useful about how high a confined surge will climb. Recomputed areas agree with the EMS published figures to 0.001 ha. The barrier lake pool polygons are not validated by any of this — EMS did not map the impoundment, and no usable satellite pass over it has appeared.

A fourth EMS area of interest exists and is deliberately kept out of the table. AOI05 Phosretar, delivered 2 September 03:21 UTC from Pleiades and Pleiades Neo imagery of 31 August, maps 422.56 ha of scoured ground along 23.9 km² of the Trishuli between Devighat and the Prithvi Highway, with 563 graded buildings (264 Destroyed), 21 bridges (11 Destroyed, including the Keurintar Hanging Bridge) and 10.44 km of road graded Destroyed. It ships in the package as `aoi_number 5`. It is not tested against the envelope because it cannot be: the AOI begins 0.99 km below the channel terminus at Devighat, and there the height-above-channel raster has no channel to measure from — its residual pixels read below zero. A naive overlay would have claimed 55.2 percent of a 35.8 ha edge slice inside the 80 m band; that number is a raster artefact and is withheld. Every AOI05 record carries `env_tested = False`, the tables above are the corridor AOIs 1–3 only, and 942.00 ha and 97.0 percent are unchanged. Extending the channel and the envelope downstream to cover Phosretar is a modelling change, not a data update, and is not done here.
